 1            After weeks of negotiation, the parties entered a joint stipulation that consented to the relief
 2 sought by Plaintiffs’ Administrative Motion (ECF No. 201-1). Without any warning to Plaintiffs

 3 during those negotiations, Capital One filed, late yesterday, a “brief” in support of Plaintiffs’

 4 Administrative Motion. (ECF No. 203.) Capital One’s brief is both procedurally improper and

 5 undermines the parties’ joint stipulation. (Id.) Despite having stipulated to the relief sought in

 6 Plaintiffs’ Administrative Motion (ECF No. 201-1), Capital One’s “support” brief transparently

 7 attempts to launder a false narrative onto the docket.1 It accuses Plaintiffs of including “false

 8 statements” in their Motion for Sanctions and refusing to “withdraw them until faced with a Rule 11

 9 motion.” (ECF No. 203 at 1-2.)

10            The record shows otherwise. Capital One concealed the technologies at issue until after the
11 close of discovery, after expert disclosures and until the eve of court-ordered depositions. As

12 catalogued in Plaintiffs’ filings, Plaintiffs’ good-faith factual descriptions of Capital One’s

13 transmissions were based on deposition testimony and Capital One’s business records. (ECF No.

14 181, pp. 10-13; ECF No. 198, pp. 7-11.) Quite literally, all Plaintiffs’ “corrected” motion adds is a

15 few words—“supposedly obfuscated”—to describe the data shared by the late-disclosed

16 technologies. Plaintiffs’ motion for administrative relief therefore does not concede any misconduct

17 by Plaintiffs. It does not change anything about Plaintiffs’ original motion at all. Rather, it reflects a

18 narrow, good-faith clarification (adding about a dozen words) to avoid Capital One’s effort to

19 misdirect from the issues in the Motion for Sanctions.

20            First, Plaintiffs’ original motion accurately described what Capital One itself produced:
21 additional server-to-server technologies that transmitted Plaintiffs’ and the putative class’s data.

22 (ECF No. 181, pp. 10-13; ECF No. 198, pp. 7-11.) In essence, Capital One quibbles about labels—

23 it contends that the data it shared was “obfuscated” and thus could not be understood by any third

24

25   1
    Plaintiffs do not wish to burden the Court with additional motion practice, but note that under Fed.
   R. Civ. P. 12(f), the Court has the authority to strike, sua sponte, “any redundant, immaterial,
26 impertinent, or scandalous matter.” That is exactly what Capital One’s “support” brief is, and the

27 Court should not hesitate to exercise its authority to strike that filing on its own. Indeed, there was
   no need for Capital One to make such filing after having stipulated to the relief in the motion, but it
28 did so anyway in a highly and unnecessarily inflammatory manner.

 1 party. Setting aside the merits of that argument, its semantic rebranding does not change the reason

 2 why Plaintiffs sought sanctions: Capital One’s failure to timely disclose these technologies.

 3 Plaintiffs’ rewording to track Capital One’s position that it obfuscates some of the data transmitted

 4 does not make the original descriptions “false.” It removes Capital One’s last refuge: arguing about

 5 adjectives rather than answering for its misconduct.

 6            Second, Capital One’s assertions concerning Rule 11 are also improper and revealing. A day

 7 after Capital One served its Rule 11 letter and draft motion, Plaintiffs identified numerous false

 8 statements and mischaracterizations based on deposition transcripts and documents produced by

 9 Capital One. In addition, Plaintiffs’ counsel warned that pressing forward would trigger § 1927

10 sanctions against the signing attorney. Shortly before the scheduled meet and confer, Capital One

11 circulated a revised Rule 11 motion to remove some of the misstatements. Then, at the meet and

12 confer, Capital One agreed to that a change to the brief to note Capital One believes the data was

13 “obfuscated” would satisfy it. To avoid burdening the Court with dueling Rule 11 and § 1927 motions

14 over the inclusion of a dozen words in a filing, which have no bearing on the underlying substance

15 of the filing, Plaintiffs agreed to the limited edits reflected in the administrative motion—i.e.,

16 describing the data shared as “supposedly obfuscated.” The absurdity of this dispute makes obvious

17 that Capital One threatened Rule 11 not because Plaintiffs’ statements were knowingly false, but

18 because Capital One wanted leverage to reframe the record after its late productions made the

19 discovery misconduct undeniable. Rule 11 is not a cudgel to retroactively sanitize discovery abuse.

20 Plaintiffs conferred2 and offered to add the allegedly clarifying language to avoid Capital One’s effort

21 to distract from its own wrongdoing and burden the Court with ancillary litigation.

22
     2
23     Capital One repeatedly chides Plaintiffs for failing to confer. (ECF No. 203 at 1.) This is yet another
     false statement by Capital One. Completely ignored by Capital One, Plaintiffs submitted an entire
24   transcript from a meet and confer, along with Capital One’s follow-up e-mail, where it confirmed
     that it refuses to supplement its discovery responses. (See ECF No. 178-2.) These documents
25   conclusively show that there was a meet and confer, and Capital One’s statements to the Court are
     false. And by now, Capital One’s conduct has given the lie to its claim that a meet and confer would
26   have resolved anything. Capital One has had plenty of opportunity to course correct. Nothing stopped
27   it from, for example, offering to supplement its production and discovery responses after the motion
     was filed, nor was Capital One prohibited from offering to meet and confer further. But it refuses to
28   do so, underscoring that it maintains its position that it will not supplement its discovery responses.

 1            Finally, Capital One’s claim that the “relief requested in Plaintiffs’ sanctions motion”

 2 changed (ECF No. 203 at 1), is not only improperly raised in its “support” brief concerning an

 3 administrative motion,3 but gets the logic exactly backwards. Plaintiffs seek to bar Capital One from

 4 opposing evidence about technologies that Capital One hid until Plaintiffs had no meaningful

 5 opportunity to test them through discovery. That is not a windfall. It is the minimum remedy

 6 necessary to prevent Capital One from benefiting from its own discovery misconduct. The prejudice

 7 Plaintiffs identified never depended on any descriptor in the corrections.4 Rather, it depended on the

 8 fact that Capital One deprived Plaintiffs of timely discovery on two server-to-server technologies

 9 that transmitted highly relevant data. Capital One’s “support” brief quietly concedes the core

10 problem: Plaintiffs were forced to litigate blindfolded and only learned the full scope of the data

11 transmissions when discovery was effectively over based on scant information that was selected by

12 Capital One for disclosure. That is the textbook case for Rule 37(c) relief. Allowing Capital One to

13 now introduce expert gloss and factual spin on technologies it concealed until discovery closed would

14 reward the very conduct Rule 37(c) deters.

15            For these reasons, the Court should disregard or strike Capital One’s filing.

 1     I.   INTRODUCTION

 2          Capital One’s opposition is an exercise in evasion. Faced with a motion grounded in belated

 3 disclosures, broken assurances, and material prejudice, Capital One avoids the merits and instead

 4 launches a barrage of collateral attacks. Capital One’s focus on rhetoric is nothing more than a sleight

 5 of hand. The issue before the Court is simple: whether Capital One complied with the Federal Rules

 6 of Civil Procedure. And based on Plaintiffs’ opening motion and Capital One’s opposition, it did not.

 7          Capital One does not dispute that, throughout fact discovery, it repeatedly represented—to

 8 Plaintiffs and to this Court—that, notwithstanding its objections, it did not withhold responsive

 9 information concerning server-to-server technologies. Those representations mattered. They resolved

10 discovery disputes, foreclosed motions to compel, defined the record on which Plaintiffs were entitled

11 to rely, and depositions and expert reports went forward. But, after discovery closed, Capital One
